content: Hello, I was wondering why Bors is used for merging pull requests when GitHub has merge ques built in?
Mathlib existed before GitHub supported merge queues, and also it doesn't support delegation and stacking (and possibly other features)

I think the key reason was batching; in the past, mathlib received more PRs per day than CI could run against, and so the answer was to stack N PRs and run CI only on the last commit. I believe the github merge queue runs the build on every commit, which was too expensive

One nice feature about bors is that when it batches multiple PRs together, it only builds it once, while (I believe) merge queue builds every PR in a batch separately/sequentially.
This was a problem especially at the end of the Lean 3 days, when building/linting mathlib would take multiple hours, and we didn't have enough runners to build every single commit (and it's a big amount of wasted compute if a PR fails CI, which regularly happens).
Mathlib has got a lot faster since then so maybe this is no longer needed, but it means we're prepared for an increase in contributions in future

I'm not sure if any maintainers have been following the github merge queue feature that closely in the last year; it's possible that it now has the batching behavior we need, but it certainly didn't when we last evaluated it.

Eric Wieser said:

it's possible that it now has the batching behavior we need

This says:

Merge limits: Select the minimum and maximum number of pull requests to merge into the base branch at the same time (between 1 and 100)

and

You can specify a minimum group size, which is useful if merges to your base branch trigger a lengthy CI build or deploy process, and you don’t want to hold up the following entries in the queue.

so it sounds like it does have batching.

Pull requests that have failed required checks can be added to a group as long as the last pull request in the group has passed required checks. If the last pull request in the group has passed required checks, this means that the checks have passed for the combined set of changes in the merge group.

This quote (from the description of "Only merge non-failing pull requests") sounds like every single PR in a group is still individually sent to CI when sent to the merge queue.

Snir Broshi said:

This says:

Merge limits: Select the minimum and maximum number of pull requests to merge into the base branch at the same time (between 1 and 100)

right below this part I find

Note
Merge limits do not combine merge_group builds. Merge limits only affect merges to the base branch once one or more merge_group has satisfied build checks.

so it sounds like it still builds each one individually but only applies the changes after a whole group is done

The examples under How merge queues work also seem to suggest that (the first 4 steps are the same between the Successful and Failing examples):

  1. User adds pull request 1 to the merge queue.
  2. The merge queue creates a temporary branch with the prefix of main/pr-1 that contains code changes from the target branch and pull request 1. A merge_group webhook event of type checks_requested is dispatched and the merge queue will await a response from your CI provider.
  3. User adds pull request 2 to the merge queue.
  4. The merge queue creates a temporary branch with the prefix of main/pr-2 that contains code changes from the target branch, pull request 1, and pull request 2, and dispatches webhooks.

Specifically, steps 2+4 suggest that builds for both PRs 1 and 2 get triggered.

There was a bit of (off-topic for that thread) discussion about bors at #mathlib4 > Technical Debt Counters @ 💬 . My opinion after thinking about the exchange there is that batching / bisection after failure might be features we could live without (especially if we don't mind spending more money on CI runners), but the delegation system is something that would take some nontrivial work (both technical and organizational) to replace.
